definition: A technique where lower-precision rounding errors are simulated in forward and backward passes during model training to minimize post-quantization accuracy loss.
details: Unlike post-training quantization (PTQ) which quantizes frozen weights, QAT incorporates low-bit representation errors directly into the training loss function, enabling the network to learn weights inherently robust to reduced precision representations.

explainer.lead: QAT simulates low-precision rounding during both forward and backward passes so the trained network is already robust to quantization. It matters because it minimizes the accuracy loss that appears after a model is actually compressed.

tiers.eli5: Like practicing a race while wearing the heavy shoes you'll actually compete in, so race day feels normal.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers insert fake-quantization operations in training so the loss accounts for low-bit error. The pitfall is cost: QAT requires full retraining, unlike post-training quantization on frozen weights.
tiers.paperLevel: Low-bit representation errors are simulated in the forward and backward passes and incorporated into the training loss, producing weights robust to reduced precision; this differs from PTQ, which quantizes frozen weights.

explainer.example: A network trained with simulated 4-bit rounding during training retains accuracy after conversion to a 4-bit representation, where a post-training approach would degrade.

citation.title: Quantizing Deep Convolutional Networks for Efficient Inference: A Whitepaper
